rv.q: There is real delicacy, too, in her mapping of Shideh’s damaged interior landscape. In her impressive final scenes, a new sort of self-exposure is required, nothing to do with headscarves but built of an emotional transparency between mother and daughter that leaves them forearmed for future battles.
What comes across keenly in this shared space is the surreal, terrifying ordeal of living in a war zone and the misery of having your life ripped away by forces beyond your control.
This is a pacy, intense, and refreshingly unusual kind of thriller – one that reminds us that the scariest things in life aren’t the ones that go bump in the night.
When it delivers the shivers, though, it comes joltingly alive.
Still, as a drama about living under the strain of war and government oppression, it absolutely works.
Under the Shadow is not just a scary play — in fact, it’s more often a rather ponderous play.
In fact, the whole production feels weirdly lightweight – despite the potency of its historical backdrop, and the enduring pertinence of its themes, given today’s geopolitical landscape.
Under the Shadow balances many different types of tension to create an intense experience that is genuinely scary and has important insights into life under war and the Iranian regime.
Nadia Latif directs Carmen Nasr’s stage adaptation of writer-filmmaker Babak Anvari’s celebrated Middle-Eastern spine tingler UNDER THE SHADOW from 2016.
Anvari's near-perfect film would be almost impossible to do justice to on stage, but Shideh's conundrum remains the stuff of nightmares.
Theatrical management of suspense is chilling.
This well-performed show reminds us of the horrific, overwhelming trauma that even people not directly physically injured by weapons can experience in a conflict zone.
It can’t sustain the delicate balance it has created – but it is undoubtedly both original and enjoyable.
The play’s monotonous rhythm is frustrating for about 70 minutes but eventually you get used to it and start to feel engaged with the characters.
Under the Shadow is proof that the stage can be every bit as scary as the cinema.
Nadia Latif's stylish, well-acted production is more nuanced – within the constraints of the genre.
Ben Stones’ design is superbly detailed with angled corridors and rooms promising eerie encounters.

cn.t: Critics find this Tehran-set horror effectively blends wartime tension with supernatural scares, praising Leila Farzad's performance and atmospheric staging, though some feel the metaphorical elements work better than the actual frights.
